cards.explanation: The answer is a great famine, friends. The text says, “So there was a great famine in Samaria.” (2 Kings 6:25) Ben-hadad, king of Aram, had marched his whole army up to besiege the city. The siege went on so long that a donkey's head sold for eighty shekels of silver.

The answer is True. During the siege of Samaria, the text says a quarter cab of dove's dung sold for five shekels of silver (2 Kings 6:25). That's a small measure of something nobody wants in their kitchen, and it still cost silver. I think that tells you exactly how hard things had gotten.

The answer is True. The king of Israel tells a woman crying out for help, “If the LORD does not help you, where can I find help for you?” (2 Kings 6:27) Then he adds a question about the threshing floor and the winepress. I think that's a king who is looking at empty hands.

The answer is that he tears his clothes. The text says, “When the king heard the words of the woman, he tore his clothes.” (2 Kings 6:30) As he passed by on the wall, the people saw the sackcloth under his clothes, right next to his skin. I think this part of the story hurts.

The answer is shut the door! Elisha, the prophet, tells the elders, “…when the messenger comes, shut the door to keep him out.” (2 Kings 6:32) He already knows what the messenger is coming for. I'd say Elisha's door policy that day was very clear.

The answer is True. Elisha asks, “Is not the sound of his master’s footsteps behind him?” (2 Kings 6:32) The messenger was sent by the king, so his master's footsteps coming right behind him means the king himself is close. Elisha sees it all coming before it shows up at the door.

The answer is False, friends. The king of Israel does not say he will keep waiting. He says, “This calamity is from the LORD. Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?” (2 Kings 6:33) He's asking why he should keep waiting. I think he's run out of patience, and that's exactly where Elisha's next words land.

The answer is cheap and plentiful, friends! Elisha says a seah of fine flour will sell for one shekel, and two seahs of barley for one shekel (2 Kings 7:1). Compare that to a donkey's head at eighty shekels of silver. That's quite a drop, and Elisha says it's coming about this time tomorrow.

The answer is eat. Elisha tells the officer who doubted the word of the LORD, “You will see it with your own eyes…” and then, “but you will not eat any of it.” (2 Kings 7:2) The officer gets a front row seat and no cookie. I mean, no flour.

The answer is the camp of the Arameans, friends. The four men say, “So come now, let us go over to the camp of the Arameans.” (2 Kings 7:4) Staying put means dying and going into the city means dying. So they take the one option that has a maybe in it.

The answer is False, friends. The four men do not find soldiers asleep. The text says that when they came to the outskirts of the camp, “…there was not a man to be found.” (2 Kings 7:5) No soldiers sleeping and no soldiers awake. Imagine walking up ready for the worst and finding an empty lot.

The answer is chariots and horses and a great army. The Lord had caused the Arameans to hear “…the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army…” (2 Kings 7:6) The Arameans said to one another that the king of Israel must have hired the kings of the Hittites and Egyptians to attack them. They took it from there.

The answer is their tents and animals, all of it. The text says the Arameans ran, “…abandoning their tents and horses and donkeys.” (2 Kings 7:7) When people run for their lives, they don't stop to pack. The four men walked into a camp with everything still in place.

The answer is True. After hiding the first load, the text says the four men entered another tent, carried off some items from there, and hid them (2 Kings 7:8). They had gone into the first tent to eat and drink, and then carried off silver, gold and clothing. I think a person in that spot can lose track of how many trips they've made.

The answer is “We are not doing what is right.” The four men say, “We are not doing what is right. Today is a day of good news.” (2 Kings 7:9) With their loot hidden, they stop and say it out loud to each other. They also say that if they wait until morning light, their sin will overtake them.

The answer is the king's household, friends. The four men say, “Now, therefore, let us go and tell the king’s household.” (2 Kings 7:9) These are men who had been sitting at the entrance of the city gate. They call out to the gatekeepers, and the gatekeepers shout the news until it's reported to the king's household (2 Kings 7:10-11).

The answer is that they left camp to hide and ambush the Israelites. That's what the king of Israel thinks. He tells his servants, “They know we are starving, so they have left the camp to hide in the field…” (2 Kings 7:12) He expects them to take the Israelites alive and walk into the city. An empty camp looked like a trap to him.

The answer is that everyone left in the city is doomed anyway. The king's servant says, “Their plight will be no worse than all the Israelites who are left here. You can see that all the Israelites here are doomed.” (2 Kings 7:13) If the scouts are in trouble, they're in no more trouble than everyone else. So he says, let's send them and find out.

The answer is False, friends. The scouts do not find a clean road. The text says they tracked the Arameans as far as the Jordan, and the whole way was littered with the clothing and equipment the Arameans had thrown off in haste (2 Kings 7:15). It looked like a very hurried departure. That's proof enough for the scouts to bring back to the king.

The answer is True. The text says, “Then the people went out and plundered the camp of the Arameans.” (2 Kings 7:16) After the scouts reported, the whole city could finally go out the gate. After all that hunger, they headed straight for the camp.

The answer is that the price drops, exactly as promised. The text says a seah of fine flour sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley sold for a shekel, “…according to the word of the LORD.” (2 Kings 7:16) That's the very price Elisha announced. Same price, same gate.

The answer is that the people trample him and he dies, and I'll say it once: this part is heavy. The text says the people trampled the officer in the gateway, and he died, just as the man of God had foretold (2 Kings 7:17). Elisha had told him, “You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it!” (2 Kings 7:2) The LORD's word held, every bit of it.
